after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =x-4 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x-4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 5 & 8 \\ u & 1 & 4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{5}^{8}\frac{-4}{(x-4)}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{-4}{u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{-4}{u}\,\text{d}u & =-4{\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(u){|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-4(\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =-4\operatorname{ln}⁡({2}^{2}) \\  & =-4\cdot 2\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =-8\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let u=8x+1, so dx=du/8 and the limits become 1 and 3. The integral is (1/8)∫₁³u^(1/2)du=[u^(3/2)/12]₁³=(3√3−1)/12, which is option c.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
We start by changing the variable:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =8x+1 \\ \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8 \\ \text{d}u & =8\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u & =\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we create a table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=8x+1.$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & \frac{1}{4} \\ u & 1 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable is

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1/4}\sqrt{8x+1}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Finally, we can solve it and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{u}\,\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{3}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot {\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\cdot \frac{2}{3}({3}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}({({3}^{3})}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(3\sqrt{3}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
